passage:
Santiago, twenty-four and babysitting for the evening, sat on the floor of the flat in Guadalajara with six-year-old Ivan, who held out a crayon drawing. In the middle of the paper was a huge black shape with two yellow eyes.
"That's scary," Santiago said, then stopped. "Tell me about it."
Ivan traced the eyes. "It lives in my wardrobe. At night it looks at me. I don't tell Mama because she says it isn't real."
Santiago nodded slowly. "It sounds really frightening. Thank you for telling me. Can we show Mama the drawing together tomorrow, and tell her it feels real to you?"
Ivan leaned in. "Okay."

qa.q: What was in the middle of Ivan's drawing?
qa.a: A huge black shape with two yellow eyes was in the middle.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling when saying "At night it looks at me"?
qa.a: Ivan was scared and had been keeping it secret. Not telling Mama because "she says it isn't real" shows Ivan felt unheard.

qa.q: What did Santiago do that gave Ivan words and trust?
qa.a: Santiago stopped, said "Tell me about it", listened and said it sounded frightening. Then Santiago offered to help tell Mama, so Ivan would not carry it alone.

qa.q: How would it feel for Ivan if Santiago had said "It isn't real"?
qa.a: Ivan would probably feel unheard again and might stop sharing. Being believed made Ivan lean in and agree to tell Mama.

grounding: A young adult hears a child describe a fear in a drawing and asks what it is about before judging, giving the child words and trust.

passage:
In the nursery cloakroom, Samir stood by the toilet door, arms wrapped round himself, not going in. Minakshi, the assistant, crouched down. She had been about to say "Come on, it's just a toilet."
Instead she asked, "What is it about the toilet, Samir?"
Samir whispered, "The hand-dryer. It shouts."
"It shouts really loudly?" Minakshi asked, and Samir nodded. "That would scare me too. Shall we look at it together first, without pressing it?"
Samir took her hand. They looked at the silver box, and Samir touched it, then giggled. Minakshi wrote a note for the lead teacher to mention to Samir's parents at pickup.

qa.q: What did Samir say scared him about the toilet?
qa.a: Samir said the hand-dryer shouts.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he stood by the door with arms wrapped round himself?
qa.a: Samir was frightened of the noise. Wrapping arms round himself and whispering shows how real the fear felt.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do instead of saying "Come on, it's just a toilet"?
qa.a: Minakshi asked what it was about, believed the fear and suggested looking at the dryer together without pressing it. She also noted it for the lead teacher to mention to the parents.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt about the urge to say "Come on"?
qa.a: Minakshi likely felt hurried and pulled toward a quick fix. Choosing to ask first gave Samir words and trust.

grounding: A young adult who hears a child's fear asks what it is about before judging, and the child finds the words.

passage:
Dear Didi,

I wanted to tell you about Eshaan's drawing before you saw it and worried.

Yesterday, while you were at work, he showed me a picture: a huge black shape with red eyes behind our building, and a tiny boy running. My first thought was to say, "Eshaan, this is too scary, draw something nice."

I stopped myself and asked, "Tell me about it. What's happening here?"

He said the black shape is the new garbage truck that comes at night. It's so loud it wakes him, and the red lights look like eyes. He thought it might come inside.

So we looked out of the window together and watched it come and go. I told him it's just a truck with a very loud engine and a driver who wants to go home.

Today he drew it again, with a smiling driver.

He said, "Masi, next time I'm scared, I'll draw it and tell you."

Love,
Anjali

qa.q: What was the black shape in Eshaan's drawing?
qa.a: The black shape is the new garbage truck that comes at night.

qa.q: What was Eshaan afraid of?
qa.a: Eshaan was scared that the loud truck with red lights like eyes might come inside the building.

qa.q: Which of Anjali's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Anjali held back the urge to say it was too scary and asked what was happening, which let Eshaan name his fear and made the fear smaller.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's mother feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and grateful that Anjali listened, and glad that Eshaan now wants to share his fears.

grounding: A young adult asks what a child's frightening drawing is about before judging, and the child trusts her with a fear.

passage:
People ask me what I learnt from a year of babysitting while I studied, and honestly, it's one thing. I'm Ishita, and I learnt it from a six-year-old called Ganga.
One night she wouldn't sleep. She kept pointing at the ceiling fan and crying. My first instinct was the grown-up one: "Ganga, fans don't hurt anyone, close your eyes." I actually had the words ready.
Instead I lay down beside her and asked, "What does the fan do that you don't like?"
She whispered that its shadow, when the fan turned, looked like hands reaching down. And that her brother had said fans can fall.
So we turned on the side lamp so the shadow went away, and I told her the fan was fixed tight, and we tugged on the hook together, standing on the bed.
She slept in ten minutes. A month later, she came to me about the bigger thing, a kid at school being mean. She said, "You always ask first."

qa.q: What did Ganga think the fan's shadow looked like?
qa.a: She said its shadow looked like hands reaching down.

qa.q: Why did Ishita hold back the words she had ready?
qa.a: Ishita sensed Ganga's fear was real and felt curious about what exactly frightened her, instead of impatient to get her to sleep.

qa.q: What would you advise an adult with a scared child at bedtime?
qa.a: Ask what exactly frightens them before reassuring, as Ishita did, then fix what you can, like turning on a lamp.

qa.q: How did Ganga come to see Ishita?
qa.a: Ganga came to trust Ishita as someone who asks first, which is why she later shared a bigger worry about school.

grounding: A young adult asks a child what her fear is about before judging, and the child later brings Ishita a bigger worry.

passage:
I live next door to Zainab and her little nephew Kiran, and my kitchen window looks right into their courtyard. Last Sunday I saw Kiran, who must be about seven, crouched over a paper, drawing hard with a black crayon. He showed it to Zainab. From where I stood it looked like a dark, scribbled storm.
I half expected her to say, "What a mess" or "Why so dark?" That's what I would have said, I think.
She didn't. She sat on the step beside him and asked something I couldn't hear. Kiran talked for a long time, pointing to parts of the paper. Once he rubbed his eyes. Zainab nodded, listened, then put an arm around him.
After a while he took a yellow crayon and added something in the corner. A sun, maybe.
I don't know what the storm was about. But Kiran went inside holding her hand, and he was chatting again.

qa.q: What was Kiran drawing with?
qa.a: He was drawing with a black crayon.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling as he talked and rubbed his eyes?
qa.a: Kiran might have been sad or upset about something the storm stood for, and relieved to be listened to.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that could help children open up?
qa.a: She sat beside Kiran and asked about the drawing instead of judging it, then listened and comforted him.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Zainab's response?
qa.a: The neighbour is struck by it, admitting they would have called it a mess, and notices Kiran was chatting again afterwards.

grounding: An observer sees a young adult ask a child about a dark drawing before judging, and the child opens up.

passage:
Monday. At the tuition table in Noor's flat, Lokesh scribbled a black shape with rows of teeth. Noor nearly said, "Draw something happier." Instead she asked, "Who's this?" "The monster under the bridge. It shouts at me." "What does it shout like?" Lokesh barked twice.
Thursday. The monster had four legs now, and a chain. "It's the big dog near the bridge," Lokesh said. "I run." Noor asked who walked with him, and that evening told his mother, who began walking him past the bridge.
The next Tuesday, Lokesh stayed after the others left. "Noor didi, can I tell you another monster? The big boys at the bus stop take my tiffin." Noor sat beside him. "Thank you for telling me. It's not your fault." She walked him home and told his mother; together they called the class teacher, who promised a teacher at the bus stop from the next morning.

qa.q: What did the monster turn out to be?
qa.a: It's the big dog near the bridge.

qa.q: Why did Noor ask "Who's this?" instead of saying "Draw something happier"?
qa.a: Noor felt curious and wanted Lokesh to feel safe explaining, not judged for a scary drawing.

qa.q: What did Noor do after hearing about the bus stop, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Noor thanked Lokesh, said it was not his fault, walked him home and called the class teacher with his mother that same day, so he was protected straight away.

qa.q: How did Noor's questions change what Lokesh was willing to share?
qa.a: Because Noor listened to the monster and the dog without judging, Lokesh trusted her enough to bring a bigger worry, the boys taking the tiffin.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking what a child's scary drawing is about before judging it, which builds the trust that lets the child bring a bigger worry later.
